flashcards.front: Why is TCP teardown four messages instead of three?
flashcards.back: Connections are full-duplex; each direction closes independently with its own FIN+ACK. After your FIN (half-close: 'no more data from me') the peer may keep sending until it sends its own FIN.

flashcards.front: What is TIME_WAIT and why 2×MSL?
flashcards.back: State held by the side sending the final ACK of teardown (~60s). Reason 1: if that ACK is lost the peer retransmits FIN and needs a re-ack. Reason 2: lets stray delayed segments die so a new connection reusing the 4-tuple can't absorb old data. SO_REUSEADDR lets servers rebind despite it.

flashcards.front: What triggers fast retransmit?
flashcards.back: Three duplicate ACKs. Cumulative ACKs repeating the same number mean later segments are arriving but one is missing — resend it immediately instead of waiting out the retransmission timeout (RTO), saving hundreds of ms.

flashcards.front: Flow control vs congestion control — one line each.
flashcards.back: Flow control protects the RECEIVER: explicit receive window (rwnd) advertised in ACKs = free buffer space. Congestion control protects the NETWORK: inferred congestion window (cwnd) probed via loss. Sender's limit = min(rwnd, cwnd).

flashcards.front: Describe slow start and AIMD in numbers.
flashcards.back: Start ~10 segments; double cwnd every loss-free RTT (slow start) until ssthresh; then +1 segment per RTT (additive increase); on loss, halve cwnd (multiplicative decrease) — the sawtooth. Timeout is harsher: cwnd back to 1, slow start again.

flashcards.front: How big must the TCP window be to fill a 1 Gbps, 50 ms RTT path?
flashcards.back: Bandwidth × delay: 1 Gbps × 0.05 s ≈ 6.25 MB in flight. The 16-bit window field caps at 64 KB, so high-BDP paths need the window-scaling option. A 64 KB window on that path yields only ~10 Mbps.

flashcards.front: What does UDP add to IP — and nothing more?
flashcards.back: Source port, destination port, length, checksum: an 8-byte header. No connection, no ACKs, no ordering, no congestion control. Datagram boundaries are preserved: one send = one receive.

flashcards.front: When does UDP beat TCP? Three families of cases.
flashcards.back: 1) Real-time media/games: retransmitted data would arrive too late to matter — skip, don't stall. 2) Tiny request/response like DNS: app-level retry is cheaper than a handshake. 3) As a substrate for custom transports — QUIC.

flashcards.front: Why does QUIC run over UDP instead of being a new IP-level protocol?
flashcards.back: Middleboxes and kernels only pass protocols they know — a new transport number would take decades to deploy. UDP passes everywhere, and userspace implementation ships with the browser. QUIC rebuilds reliability per-stream, fuses TLS 1.3 (1-RTT, 0-RTT resumed), and survives IP changes via connection IDs.

flashcards.front: Walk the cold-cache DNS resolution chain for app.example.com.
flashcards.back: Stub resolver → recursive resolver → root server (referral to .com TLD) → TLD server (referral to the domain's authoritative NS) → authoritative server returns the A record. The recursive resolver caches every step per TTL.

flashcards.front: Why do DNS changes 'propagate slowly', and what's the ops trick before a migration?
flashcards.back: Nothing is pushed: caches everywhere serve the old record until its TTL expires. Trick: lower the TTL (e.g. 3600→60) well before the change so the eventual switch strands users for at most the new TTL.

flashcards.front: A vs AAAA vs CNAME vs MX vs NS vs TXT — one phrase each.
flashcards.back: A: name→IPv4. AAAA: name→IPv6. CNAME: alias to another name (a CNAME name may hold no other records — so no CNAME at the zone apex). MX: mail servers + priority. NS: authoritative servers for the zone. TXT: free text (SPF, ownership proofs).

flashcards.front: Head-of-line blocking in HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 — where does it live?
flashcards.back: 1.1: at the HTTP layer — one exchange at a time per connection (hence 6 parallel connections). 2: solved in HTTP via multiplexed streams, but moved into TCP — one lost packet stalls ALL streams (ordered byte stream). 3/QUIC: ordering is per-stream, loss stalls only its own stream.

flashcards.front: Name HTTP/2's three headline features over 1.1.
flashcards.back: Multiplexing (many streams as interleaved binary frames on one TCP connection), HPACK header compression (cookies/UA repeat every request), stream prioritization. One connection also means one handshake and one congestion-control ramp.

flashcards.front: In the TLS handshake, what single check actually kills a MITM?
flashcards.back: The server signs the handshake transcript with the certificate's PRIVATE key. A MITM can replay the public certificate but cannot produce that signature, and no honest CA will certify a domain he doesn't control. Cert chain + name check + proof-of-possession = authentication.

flashcards.front: What does a passive observer still see on an HTTPS connection?
flashcards.back: Destination IP, hostname (cleartext SNI in ClientHello — until ECH), packet timing and sizes. Hidden: path, query, headers, cookies, both bodies. 'ISP knows you're on youtube.com, not which video.'

flashcards.front: What is forward secrecy and which mechanism provides it?
flashcards.back: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE): fresh key pairs per connection derive the session secret, which is never stored. Stealing the server's long-term key later cannot decrypt recorded past traffic.

flashcards.front: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite — which attack does each cookie flag block?
flashcards.back: HttpOnly: JavaScript can't read the cookie — blocks XSS session theft. Secure: sent only over HTTPS — blocks plaintext capture. SameSite=Lax/Strict: not attached to cross-site requests — blocks CSRF.

flashcards.front: Session-ID cookie vs JWT — the core tradeoff in one line.
flashcards.back: Session ID: state server-side, lookup per request, instant revocation, needs a shared store. JWT: signed claims client-side, stateless verification, easy scaling, but irrevocable until expiry — hence short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens.

flashcards.front: Who enforces CORS, and whom does it protect?
flashcards.back: The BROWSER enforces it, protecting USERS (whose cookies ride on cross-origin requests). curl and server-to-server calls ignore it — CORS is not API access control. Often the response reached the browser, which refused to hand it to JS.

flashcards.front: When does the browser send a CORS preflight, and what is it?
flashcards.back: An OPTIONS request sent before non-simple requests (methods like PUT/DELETE, or headers like Authorization/Content-Type: application/json), asking Access-Control-Request-Method/Headers. The real request goes only if the server's Access-Control-Allow-* response approves.

flashcards.front: How does NAPT let one public IP serve a whole network?
flashcards.back: The router rewrites each outbound packet's source private-IP:port to public-IP:unique-port and keeps a translation table; replies to that port are mapped back inside. Inbound-without-mapping is dropped — hence port forwarding for servers and STUN/TURN for peer-to-peer.

flashcards.front: What do STUN and TURN each do for a video call behind NAT?
flashcards.back: STUN: a public server reports your public IP:port so both peers can attempt hole punching (simultaneous outbound sends create NAT mappings for each other). TURN: a public relay that carries the media when hole punching fails under strict NATs.

flashcards.front: What does accept() return, and what port is the new connection on?
flashcards.back: A NEW socket/fd for that one established client connection (handshake already completed by the kernel into the accept queue). Same server port as the listener, which stays open and listening. The random ephemeral port belongs to the CLIENT side.

flashcards.front: How do 10,000 connections share server port 443 without mixing bytes?
flashcards.back: A connection is identified by the 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port); the kernel demultiplexes every segment on the full tuple. The real concurrency ceiling is file descriptors and buffer memory, not '65535 ports'.

flashcards.front: What limits does listen(backlog) set and what happens on overflow?
flashcards.back: Backlog caps the accept queue of fully-handshaken connections awaiting accept(). When it overflows under load, new handshakes are dropped or refused — clients see timeouts/connection resets while the app is too slow to accept().
